chapters.title: Chapter 4: Calls, Covered Calls, and Collars

lessons.title: Hedging the Fear of Missing Out: Calls for Investors Sitting in Cash

children.text: Every hedge so far has protected money already in the market. But one of the most painful risks an investor faces is the opposite: money sitting outside the market while it runs away. The bonus that arrived in March, the plot you sold, the FD maturing in two months. Invest it all today and the market might fall 10% next week. Wait, and the market might rise 10% while you watch. Most people freeze and do nothing for a year. This lesson shows how a call option lets you put a ceiling on the price you will pay to enter, while your cash stays safely parked, and when simpler tools do the job better.

body.text: For an investor holding cash, the risk is a rally, not a crash. Buying a call caps the level at which you effectively enter the market, while the cash earns interest. It is the protective put's mirror image.

markDefs.definition: Systematic Transfer Plan: an instruction to move a fixed amount at regular intervals from one mutual fund, usually a liquid or debt fund, into another, usually an equity fund, within the same fund house.

children.text: An investor with a lump sum has three basic choices. Invest it all now and accept the risk of a fall right after. Spread it over several months, often through an

from a liquid fund, and accept that a rally in the meantime raises your average entry. Or keep the cash parked and buy call options that pay off if the market rises before you invest. The third choice is the one this lesson is about, and it only makes sense in specific situations.
How a Call Caps Your Entry Level

Buy a Nifty call with a notional value that matches the amount you plan to invest. If the Nifty rises above the strike before you invest, the call gains a rupee for every point above it, which offsets the higher price you now pay for your index fund. If the Nifty falls, the call expires worthless, but you invest at a lower level. Your worst effective entry level is fixed on the day you buy the call.

body.caption: K = call strike, C = call premium in index points. Interest earned on the parked cash partly offsets C.

children.text: Worked Example: The Plot Sale Proceeds

Neelam, 42, a school principal in Chandigarh, has just received ₹32,50,000 from selling a family plot. She wants to move it into a Nifty 50 index fund, but the market is at 25,000 and she is torn. Her adviser suggests parking the money in a liquid fund for three months while she decides, and buying two lots (130 units) of the three-month 26,000 call at ₹390 in case the market runs away.

body.title: Three ways to handle a lump sum over three months

children.text: Path C has the same shape as a protective put on a portfolio: a flat floor on the left and rising participation on the right. In a fall, Neelam keeps her cash almost intact and can invest at a lower level. In a strong rally, the calls recover most of what path B misses. At 28,000, path C is ₹2,09,300 ahead of simply waiting, though still ₹1,27,900 behind having invested on day one. That gap is roughly the 26,000 strike's ₹1,30,000 deductible, less a little.

body.text: Notice that the interest on the parked cash, about ₹52,800, roughly paid for the ₹50,700 of calls. That is not a coincidence. Holding cash plus a call is economically very close to holding the index plus a put, a relationship called put-call parity that you saw in Chapter 2, Lesson 3. The interest you earn by not being invested is part of what makes the call affordable. When interest rates are high, this approach is relatively cheaper.

body.title: Your worst entry level
body.prompt: With the Nifty at 25,000, an investor holding cash buys the three-month 25,500 call at ₹610. What is the maximum effective Nifty level at which they will end up entering the market, ignoring interest on their cash?
body.explanation: Maximum effective entry = strike + premium = 25,500 + 610 = 26,110. However high the Nifty goes, the call's payoff above 25,500 offsets the extra cost of buying in, and the ₹610 premium is the price of that protection.

body.title: The mirror image
body.textWithBlank: Holding cash and buying a call creates a payoff shape very similar to owning the index and buying a protective ___.
body.explanation: Both combinations have a floor below and open-ended participation above. The difference in cost between them is mostly the interest earned on the cash, which is the essence of put-call parity.

body.caption: Choosing how to deploy a lump sum

cells: Nothing upfront, but full exposure to an immediate fall
Long horizons where short-term timing matters little

Most investors. Simple, no F&O account, and removes the timing decision
Premium, partly offset by interest on the cash

Money not yet received, plus calls

body.text: The call only covers its own window. When it expires, Neelam still has to invest the money. If the Nifty has fallen to 22,000, she must actually buy then, when the news is likely to be frightening. If she lets the calls expire and keeps waiting, she has paid ₹50,700 for nothing. A call-based plan must include a firm date and rule for putting the money to work.

body.title: A legitimate use of calls?
body.question: Which of these is the clearest example of using calls as a hedge rather than a bet?
options: A salaried investor with ₹2 lakh in savings buys four lots of Nifty calls because a friend expects a rally.
An investor whose ₹16 lakh FD matures in six weeks, and who plans to invest it in a Nifty index fund, buys one lot of a two-month Nifty call.
An investor fully invested in equity funds buys Nifty calls to double their exposure before the Budget.
A trader buys weekly Bank Nifty calls every Tuesday.
body.explanation: The FD investor has a specific, near-certain amount arriving soon, an intention to invest it in the Nifty, and a hedge sized to that amount with an expiry that covers the gap. The others have no matching future exposure: they are adding leveraged exposure they cannot back with real money.

body.title: The FD that matures in two months
body.scenario: Rahul, 36, a government doctor in Bhubaneswar, has a ₹16 lakh FD maturing in eight weeks. Breaking it early would cost a penalty. He has decided to put the full amount into a Nifty 50 index fund when it matures. The Nifty is at 25,000 and has been rising steadily. With a lot size of 65, one lot is ₹16,25,000 of exposure. He is considering buying one lot of a two-month 25,500 call at about ₹340, costing ₹22,100.
body.prompt: Is this a sensible hedge for Rahul? What should he check, and what could go wrong?
body.modelAnswer:
1. It is a reasonable use of a call. The exposure is real, the amount is known, the date is fixed, and one lot of ₹16.25 lakh is a close match for ₹16 lakh.
2. His maximum effective entry is 25,500 + 340 = 25,840. If the Nifty rallies to 27,000 before maturity, the call pays about (27,000 − 25,500) × 65 = ₹97,500, offsetting most of the higher price.
3. The cost is ₹22,100, about 1.4% of the amount, with no interest to offset it because his money is still locked in the FD, which is earning its own interest anyway.
4. Things to check: that the call's expiry falls on or after his FD maturity, that he will actually invest on maturity rather than wait for a dip, and that he understands he could lose the full ₹22,100 if the market does not rise.
5. What could go wrong: if the FD is delayed, or he changes his mind about investing, the call becomes a pure bet. And if the market falls, he loses the premium, although he then invests at a lower level.
6. The simpler alternative is to accept the timing risk and invest through an STP over six months after maturity. For many investors, that is good enough and needs no F&O account.
The lesson: a call is a hedge only when real money, a real date and a real intention stand behind it.

body.title: Why not just buy the index fund plus a put?

children.text: You could. Investing the full amount in an index fund and buying puts gives a very similar shape to holding cash and buying calls. The practical differences decide which is better for you:

Index fund plus put: you earn dividends, the money is already invested so there is no second decision, and there is no liquid fund tax to consider. But you face basis risk if you do not use a pure Nifty fund, and exit loads if you change your mind early.

Cash plus call: the money stays liquid and safe, and you keep full flexibility to choose a different fund later. But you earn interest instead of dividends, and you still have to make the investment decision when the call expires.
If you are sure you want to be invested and only fear a fall, invest and buy puts. If you are unsure when or where to invest and fear a rally more, keep cash and buy calls.

body.title: Before using calls to hedge cash on the sidelines
steps: Confirm the money is real and available, or near-certain to arrive by a known date, and that you intend to invest it in something that tracks the Nifty.
Match the notional value of the calls to the amount you will invest, and never exceed it.
Pick an expiry that covers the full waiting window, and a strike whose maximum effective entry level you can accept.
Compare the premium with the interest your cash will earn, and with the simpler option of an STP.
Write down the date on which you will invest regardless of where the market is, and keep that commitment.

cards.definition: The risk that the market rises while you are holding cash you plan to invest.
Call strike + premium. The highest level at which you effectively enter, however far the market rises.
Buying calls ahead of money you are certain to receive and invest, to protect against a rally before it arrives.
Systematic Transfer Plan. Moves money in fixed instalments from a liquid or debt fund into an equity fund.
The link showing that cash plus a call behaves much like the index plus a put, with interest explaining the cost difference.

points: For money waiting to be invested, the risk is a rally. A call caps your effective entry level at strike plus premium.
Cash plus a call has the same shape as the index plus a protective put. Interest on the cash offsets much of the call's cost.
Size the calls to the money you will actually invest, with an expiry that covers the full waiting window.
Calls also work for money not yet received, such as a maturing FD, but only if it is near-certain and you will invest it.
A call-based plan still needs a firm date to invest. Letting calls expire and continuing to wait wastes the premium.
For most investors, an STP is simpler and good enough. Calls suit large sums and short, defined windows.

Option premiums, liquid fund returns and investor examples are illustrative, and the comparisons ignore dividends, taxes and transaction charges. Returns on liquid funds are not guaranteed. Consult a SEBI-registered investment adviser before deploying a lump sum or using options.
